name: Berkeley high-resistivity silicon detector process
description: Lawrence Berkeley Laboratory fabricated p-i-n radiation detector diodes and p-channel transistors on the same high-resistivity silicon wafer, using backside gettering to limit diode leakage while retaining compatibility with integrated-circuit processing.

date.basis: Month of issue in the Department of Energy's OSTI metadata. Exact fabrication date is unresolved.

events.statement: A Berkeley laboratory report documented the process and characterization of p-i-n diodes fabricated on the same high-resistivity silicon wafer as test transistors.

evidence.supports: The earlier report documents working devices and their leakage performance.

events.statement: Steve Holland published the fabrication and electrical characterization of the low-leakage detector process.

evidence.supports: The author reports the fabrication approach, paired diode and transistor fabrication, and the role of backside gettering at Lawrence Berkeley Laboratory.

earliest_record.rationale: The dated preprint already reports the measured devices. The journal article is a later publication.

why: Readout close to the detectors was important for high-energy physics. A fabrication process compatible with integrated circuits allowed tests of detector and transistor fabrication on the same wafer.
caveats: The paired devices were a fabrication demonstration. The paper stops short of reporting a complete monolithically integrated detector and readout system.

links.statement: The Berkeley detector process and Hu's earlier IBM process both used deposited backside polysilicon as an impurity sink. Berkeley doped the layer with phosphorus and used it as the diode's back contact.
links.scope: Deposited polysilicon as an extrinsic getter during fabrication.
links.caveats: Holland cites Hu when explaining polysilicon gettering. The influence of Hu's individual process on Berkeley's full fabrication sequence remains unresolved.

evidence.supports: Cites Hu for backside polysilicon and describes the Berkeley process using a phosphorus-doped layer for both gettering and the diode's back contact.
Hu describes deposited backside polysilicon as an impurity sink in integrated circuit processing.
Different experiments also tested the use of a backside polysilicon impurity sink and place Hu's earlier patent in the same technique family.
